Can You Get Dental Implants If You Have a History of Repeated Jaw Fractures?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

For many adults living with the long-term effects of repeated jaw fractures, the prospect of restoring missing teeth can feel uncertain. One of the most common questions patients bring to dental consultations is whether their jaw history might prevent them from being suitable candidates for dental implants.

It is entirely understandable to search online for answers before booking a consultation. Understanding what dental implants require — and how previous jaw injuries might affect the process — can help patients feel better prepared and more confident about exploring their options.

This article provides a clear, educational overview of dental implants for patients with a history of jaw fractures. It explores what factors dentists consider during the assessment process, how jaw bone health relates to implant success, and what steps may help patients with complex histories move forward with treatment planning. Professional dental advice remains essential for anyone with individual concerns.

Can You Get Dental Implants With a History of Jaw Fractures?

Dental implants for patients with a history of jaw fractures may still be possible, but suitability depends entirely on individual clinical assessment. Factors such as bone density, healing quality, and fracture location are carefully evaluated. Some patients may require preparatory treatment before implants can be considered. A thorough examination is always necessary.

Understanding Jaw Fractures and Their Impact on Bone Structure

A jaw fracture, clinically known as a mandibular or maxillary fracture, occurs when one of the bones of the jaw sustains a break or crack — typically as a result of trauma such as a fall, sporting injury, or accident. When fractures occur repeatedly, the cumulative effect on the jaw bone can be more significant than a single isolated incident.

Repeated fractures may affect the jaw in several ways. The bone may heal with altered density or irregular architecture in the repaired areas. In some cases, scar tissue forms around fracture sites, which can behave differently from healthy bone tissue. There may also be subtle changes to the blood supply in affected areas, which plays an important role in how well bone supports healing processes over time.

For dental implants to integrate successfully, the jawbone must have sufficient volume and density to anchor the titanium implant post securely. This process, known as osseointegration, relies on healthy, living bone tissue responding to the implant and fusing around it over several months.

If repeated fractures have affected bone quality in the areas where implants might be placed, this becomes an important clinical consideration — though it does not automatically mean implants are unsuitable. Every patient's history is different, and professional assessment is essential to understand the individual picture.

How Dentists Assess Implant Suitability After Jaw Fractures

When a patient with a history of jaw fractures attends a dental implant consultation, the clinician will conduct a thorough and structured assessment. This is not a simple yes-or-no process — it involves gathering detailed information about the patient's dental, medical, and injury history alongside clinical and radiographic examination.

Key aspects of this assessment typically include:

Radiographic imaging: Dental X-rays and, in many cases, cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans provide detailed three-dimensional images of the jaw bone. This helps the dentist evaluate bone volume, density, and the precise locations of any previous fracture sites or surgical hardware that may have been used in repair.

Medical and surgical history review: The dentist will want to understand how many fractures occurred, when they happened, how they were treated, and how well the bone appeared to heal. Any previous jaw surgeries are also relevant.

Assessment of systemic health: Conditions such as osteoporosis, diabetes, or autoimmune disorders can influence bone quality and healing capacity, and are always considered alongside a trauma history.

Gum and soft tissue assessment: The health of the gum tissue and the quality of the soft tissue overlying potential implant sites is also evaluated.

This comprehensive approach helps the dental team build an accurate picture of whether implant placement may be feasible, and whether any preparatory steps would be beneficial.

The Science of Osseointegration: Why Bone Quality Matters

To understand why jaw fracture history is clinically relevant, it helps to appreciate what happens during dental implant integration at a biological level.

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is placed into the jawbone to serve as an artificial tooth root. Titanium is used because of its unique biocompatibility — the human body generally does not reject it, and bone tissue actively grows around and fuses to the implant surface over time. This fusion process is called osseointegration.

For osseointegration to occur reliably, the bone surrounding the implant needs to be of sufficient quality. Bone is a living tissue composed of a mineralised matrix and cells including osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) and osteoclasts (bone-remodelling cells). When a fracture heals, the body works to reconstruct bone, but the result is not always identical to the original structure.

In cases of repeated fractures, certain areas of the jaw may exhibit:

  • Reduced bone density in previously fractured zones
  • Altered trabecular architecture — the internal lattice-like structure of bone
  • Areas of fibrous non-union — where bone did not fully reconnect and fibrous tissue remains instead
  • Compromised vascularity — reduced blood vessel supply, which is critical for bone healing and implant integration

Where these changes are present, a dentist experienced in complex implant cases will carefully evaluate whether the bone can support an implant, whether bone augmentation may help, or whether implant placement in a different anatomical position might be more appropriate.

If you would like to understand more about how implants work structurally, our overview of dental implant treatment options and costs provides a helpful starting point.

Bone Grafting and Augmentation: Rebuilding the Foundation

For patients whose jaw fracture history has resulted in bone loss or compromised bone quality, bone grafting and augmentation procedures may offer a pathway towards implant treatment. These procedures aim to rebuild or supplement the existing bone in areas where it is insufficient to reliably support an implant.

Bone grafting in dental implant planning can take several forms:

Autogenous bone graft: Bone is taken from another area of the patient's own body — often from the chin, the back of the jaw, or the hip — and placed at the implant site. This is often preferred as the patient's own bone may integrate well, though outcomes vary between individuals.

Allograft: Processed donor bone from a bone bank is used. This removes the need for a second surgical site.

Synthetic or xenograft materials: Artificial or animal-derived bone substitute materials can also be used to stimulate bone regeneration.

Guided bone regeneration (GBR): A resorbable or non-resorbable membrane may be placed over a graft site to encourage bone growth and prevent soft tissue from occupying the space.

These procedures add time to the overall treatment journey, as the grafted site typically requires several months to consolidate before implant placement. However, they can meaningfully improve conditions in areas previously affected by fractures.

Whether bone augmentation is appropriate depends on the extent of the deficiency and the patient's overall health. This is always evaluated on an individual basis. Patients with substantial bone loss may also find our guide on implants with severe bone loss useful for background reading before consultation.

Factors That May Influence Implant Planning in Patients With Fracture History

Not all patients with a history of jaw fractures will face identical challenges. Several factors influence the complexity of the clinical picture and how a dentist might approach treatment planning:

Number and severity of previous fractures: A single well-healed fracture from many years ago may have minimal impact on implant suitability. Repeated fractures, particularly in the same anatomical area, are more likely to have created localised changes in bone structure.

Location of fracture sites relative to implant sites: If previous fractures occurred in areas of the jaw where teeth are not missing, they may be less directly relevant to implant placement. Conversely, fractures in the precise area where an implant is needed require careful evaluation.

Presence of surgical hardware: Some patients who have undergone jaw fracture repair have plates, screws, or wires remaining in the jaw. These may influence implant positioning and must be accounted for in treatment planning.

Time elapsed since fractures: Older injuries that have fully healed are generally evaluated more straightforwardly than recent or incompletely healed fractures.

Smoking status: Smoking has a well-documented negative effect on bone healing and implant integration. For patients with an already complex bone history, smoking cessation is typically strongly encouraged.

Systemic health: As noted previously, conditions affecting bone metabolism or immune response are considered carefully.

A thorough consultation allows the dental team to understand these nuances and provide guidance that genuinely reflects the individual patient's situation.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

Patients who have experienced repeated jaw fractures and are considering tooth replacement should seek a professional dental assessment when they feel ready to explore their options. There are also specific circumstances where attending sooner may be advisable.

Consider arranging a dental consultation if you are experiencing:

  • Persistent discomfort or aching in the jaw — particularly in areas associated with previous injuries
  • Difficulty chewing or biting related to missing teeth or jaw changes
  • Changes in bite alignment that have developed since a jaw injury
  • Numbness or altered sensation in the jaw, lip, or chin area, which may indicate nerve involvement
  • Swelling, tenderness, or signs of infection around any previously treated jaw sites
  • Looseness or discomfort around existing dental restorations that may have been affected by jaw changes

None of these experiences should cause alarm, but they are all worth discussing with a dental professional. Early assessment tends to provide more treatment options and allows any necessary preparatory steps to be planned carefully.

Dental symptoms and concerns related to a trauma history can be complex, and a clinician who understands your full history will be best placed to advise you.

Prevention and Oral Health Maintenance for Patients With Complex Jaw Histories

While it is not always possible to prevent jaw fractures — particularly those arising from accidents or trauma — there are practical steps that patients with a complex jaw history can take to support their oral health and protect their long-term dental wellbeing.

Attend regular dental check-ups: Consistent preventive dental care allows your dentist to monitor bone health, gum condition, and the stability of any existing restorations. This is particularly valuable when jaw history adds complexity to your dental picture.

Maintain thorough daily oral hygiene: Brushing twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste, flossing, and using interdental brushes helps protect the health of gum tissue and natural teeth — the foundation of any implant treatment.

Avoid smoking: If you smoke, the evidence is clear that smoking impairs bone healing and significantly reduces the predictability of dental implant integration. Smoking cessation support is widely available in London.

Protect your jaw from further injury: If you participate in contact sports or activities with a risk of facial trauma, wearing a properly fitted mouthguard can help reduce the risk of further jaw injuries.

Discuss medications with your dentist: Some medications — including certain bisphosphonates used for osteoporosis — can affect bone metabolism and must be disclosed to your dental team, as they have implications for implant planning.

Eat a balanced diet: Adequate intake of calcium, vitamin D, and phosphorus supports bone health. Your GP can advise on whether supplementation is appropriate if you have concerns about bone density.

Explore our guidance on dental implant maintenance for additional practical advice.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants may still be an option for patients with a history of repeated jaw fractures, but individual clinical assessment is essential to determine suitability.
  • Bone quality and volume at the planned implant site are critical factors — previous fractures can affect these, but the extent varies significantly between patients.
  • Comprehensive assessment, including CBCT imaging and a detailed medical and trauma history review, is the foundation of appropriate implant planning in complex cases.
  • Bone grafting and augmentation procedures can help rebuild insufficient bone in previously fractured areas, potentially creating conditions suitable for implant placement.
  • Other health factors such as smoking, systemic health conditions, and medication use are also taken into account alongside jaw fracture history.
  • Regular dental care and good oral hygiene remain important for all patients, including those with complex jaw histories, as they support the best possible foundation for any future treatment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a history of jaw fractures automatically rule out dental implants?

No — a history of jaw fractures does not automatically disqualify a patient from dental implant treatment. What matters is the current state of the jawbone in the area where implants would be placed. Dentists assess bone density, volume, and quality on an individual basis. In some cases, preparatory treatment such as bone grafting may be recommended to improve conditions before implant placement is considered. Every patient's situation is unique, and suitability is determined through thorough clinical examination rather than history alone.

How long after a jaw fracture should I wait before considering dental implants?

There is no universal timeframe, as healing varies significantly between individuals and depends on the severity and location of the fracture. Generally, clinicians prefer to allow sufficient time for bone to consolidate and stabilise following a fracture before commencing implant treatment. This is typically at least several months, but may be longer. Your dental and medical teams will advise based on your specific circumstances, including imaging assessment of how well the fracture site has healed.

Will the dentist need to see my previous jaw fracture treatment records?

It is very helpful for your dentist to have access to relevant records, including any surgical reports, imaging, and details of how your fractures were managed. If surgical hardware such as plates or screws was placed during fracture repair, this is particularly important for implant planning. You can usually request records from the hospital or surgical team that treated you. Your dental practice can advise on what information would be most useful to bring to your consultation.

Can bone grafting overcome the bone loss caused by jaw fractures?

Bone grafting procedures can often help rebuild bone volume and quality in areas affected by previous fractures or bone loss. However, the success of grafting depends on factors including the extent of deficiency, the patient's overall health, and how well the graft site heals. Grafting adds additional stages to the treatment journey, typically several months for consolidation before implant placement. Whether grafting is appropriate is assessed individually. It is not suitable or necessary for all patients, and outcomes cannot be guaranteed.

Are dental implants safe for people who have had jaw surgery?

Dental implants can be considered for patients who have previously undergone jaw surgery, but the surgical history is an important part of the assessment. The presence of plates, screws, or other hardware, scar tissue, and changes to bone architecture following surgery are all taken into account during planning. In some cases, specialist referral or a multidisciplinary approach involving an oral and maxillofacial surgeon may be recommended. Safety and appropriateness are evaluated on a case-by-case basis during a comprehensive clinical assessment.

What questions should I ask at my dental implant consultation if I have a jaw fracture history?

It can be helpful to prepare questions in advance. You might ask: How will my fracture history affect where implants can be placed? What imaging will be taken and what will it show? Is bone grafting likely to be needed in my case? How long might treatment take given my history? Are there any specific risks I should be aware of? Will my dentist liaise with the surgeon who treated my fractures? Being open about your full history — including dates of injuries, treatments received, and any ongoing symptoms — will help the clinical team give you the most accurate and useful guidance. You can find further information about what to expect during a first implant consultation on our website.

Conclusion

A history of repeated jaw fractures understandably raises questions about whether dental implants are a realistic option. The honest and reassuring answer is that a fracture history does not automatically close the door on implant treatment — but it does make thorough, individualised clinical assessment all the more important.

Dental implants for patients with a history of jaw fractures require careful evaluation of bone quality, imaging review, and consideration of the full medical and surgical history. For some patients, the jaw bone may be in excellent condition despite previous fractures. For others, preparatory steps such as bone grafting may be recommended before implants are placed. In all cases, the clinical picture is unique to the individual.

If you have experienced repeated jaw fractures and are thinking about tooth replacement, taking the step of arranging a specialist consultation is the most constructive thing you can do. A qualified clinician can assess your individual situation accurately and outline the options that may realistically be available to you.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.
